Years of Spiritual Awareness

I didn't set out to be a teacher. I set out to understand people and make children understand — why we struggle, why we light up, why some knowledge transforms lives while other knowledge simply sits on a shelf. Teaching found me, and I found my soul's journey inside it.

"Where inquiry meets empathy, and learning becomes a way of being."

I am Shanmukha, an educator driven by inquiry, research, and meaningful learning experiences. My work spans facilitating Global Perspectives (Cambridge, Grades 8–12) and transitioning into Individuals and Societies (IB MYP, Grades 6–8). Regardless of the curriculum, I focus on building inquiry skills, research thinking, and project-based learning grounded in real-world contexts.

Over the past four years in education, I have come to deeply understand the importance of exposing children to diverse models of learning — varied pedagogies, curricula, skills, and subjects. When these experiences are combined with attention to social-emotional, physical, mental, and spiritual well-being — especially in the early years up to Grade 10 — they nurture lifelong learners who are open to growth, exploration, and self-discovery.

Before stepping into formal teaching, I pursued a B.Tech in Aerospace Engineering. Those years sparked a deeper philosophical inquiry into life, childhood, and the inner child within each of us. This curiosity led me to the Gandhi Fellowship, where I worked with tribal children, families, and communities in Singrauli, Madhya Pradesh — an experience that grounded me in local realities and prompted me to question the effectiveness of mainstream educational policies.

Seeking deeper understanding, I pursued a Master of Arts in Education from Azim Premji University. Over nearly a decade of reflection and exploration, I have come to see life itself as a school — and each of us as learners on a continuous journey.

I am deeply invested in the well-being of children, adults, and the larger ecosystem. I believe in nurturing the five dimensions of being: physical, intellectual, emotional, social, and spiritual. At the core, I value love, awareness, and conscious living — choosing understanding over ego, and connection over individualism.

My Philosophy

Four beliefs that hold everything together

01

Earth is a School

All beings come to Earth for learning and we learn from our birth to our last breath. Our planet is not just made of five elements — Air, Water, Soil, Fire, Space — it also contains the profound wisdom these elements and our souls bring. That's why Earth is not just a living planet, it's a learning planet. And that's why we all are lifelong learners.

02

School is for Life

Children learn from spaces they trust. Before any curriculum, we must invest deeply in the quality of connection — with students, parents, and communities. Safety is the soil from which genuine curiosity grows, and lays the foundation for children to trust themselves, build confidence, and excel in the path they take.

03

Living Questions

Where there is freedom to ask questions, there is freedom to think deeper and make meaningful connections. I am suspicious of teachers who only give answers. The most profound education happens when we model genuine uncertainty — when we show children that not-knowing is not a failure, but the beginning of thinking.

04

Meaningful Wholeness

Open-ended thinking, when supported by a healthy and nurturing environment, fosters meaningful connections. Students begin to see subjects, activities, sports, arts, labs, and all experiences not as separate entities, but as interconnected parts of a whole — a wholesome "meal" that nourishes all dimensions of child growth.

Programs

Spaces I hold for learning together

📖

Young Researcher's Program

A thoughtfully designed introduction to research for students in Grades 8–12. It empowers learners to move beyond rote learning and develop critical thinking, inquiry, research, and effective communication — and most importantly, a love for knowledge and research.

Students learn how to ask meaningful questions, investigate real-world topics, and present ideas with clarity. The program bridges CBSE/ICSE and international approaches (IB/Cambridge) by fostering independent thinking and application-based learning. Students create their own research report and presentation by the end.

Online 4 Weeks Grade 8–12

Education & Critical Thinking

The Invisible Bridge: Where IB and Cambridge Quietly Converge

Shanmukha Munagala · April 2026 · 8 min read

Surprisingly, I found core similarities between the IB mission statement and the subject I teach in Cambridge — Global Perspectives. IB aims to develop inquiring, knowledgeable and caring youngsters who develop understanding, acceptance and respect for diverse cultures and perspectives for co-creating a peaceful world. Similarly, Global Perspectives as a subject in Cambridge intends to create the same approach for students.

GP/GPR in IGCSE and AS/A levels have a set of learnings and objectives that match with the core elements of IBDP. While Extended Essay matches with the Research Report and Individual Reports, Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS) matches with the team projects of IGCSE and AS levels. They both serve the purpose of promoting intercultural understanding and perspective, and introducing local, national and global perspectives that make students global citizens with international mindedness.

“The core difference I observed is that many schools treat GP as an optional and special subject — when in truth, it carries the very skills the world demands.”

Upon my continuous reflection on the skills and values that this subject can impart on learners, I understood that the rest of the mainstream subjects in Cambridge curriculum — Mathematics, Sciences and Humanities — don’t cater much to learner profiles like inquirers, communicators, principled, open-minded, caring, risk-taking, balanced and reflective. Though there is extensive scope to weave these characteristic traits into any mainstream subject, the exams and activities in Cambridge don’t focus extensively on these skills other than in GP.

This created an unnecessary gap between learners and GP, creating an opinion on the subject as a tough and heavy subject — rather than normalising the learning of research, evaluation, analysis, reflection, critical thinking and problem solving through coursework like Team Projects, Individual Reports, Essays and Written Papers. Whereas IB treats these skills as core objectives and ensures that students are ready for lifelong learning, irrespective of their subject choices.

IB’s Reverse Engineering Approach

The IB initially began with the Diploma Programme and later ideated the MYP and PYP in 1994 and 1997 respectively — a move that reveals a great deal about its philosophy. This reverse engineering approach ensures a continuum where students’ readiness for the world as young adults is always the guiding priority. The IB laid out characteristic traits that are relevant to all students across the globe: international mindedness.

Entry Profile

  1. Students are aware of who they are, their roots, history and different ways of expressing themselves.
  2. Students develop respect and care for themselves, others and the entire ecosystem.
  3. They become comfortable with intercultural relationships, personal and cultural expression.
  4. Students have a strong foundation in scientific and technical skills with focus on sustainability, development, equality and humaneness.

Competencies Developed

  1. Students are able to enjoy their learning journey and the expression of their learnings.
  2. Students are capable of critical, creative and ethical thinking — identifying different perspectives, finding correlations between local, national and global standards, and questioning information for its credibility.
  3. Students become familiar with research and communication skills. They ask the right questions, manage sources, and write clearly and confidently — whether an argumentative essay or a personal reflection.
  4. Students grow comfortable with social and self-management skills: regulating emotions, nurturing empathy, building relationships and finding purpose.

Personal Qualities That Benefit an IBDP Student

  1. Enthusiasm to learn new things and concepts.
  2. Enjoyment in dealing with complex problems and finding solutions.
  3. Engagement with different perspectives and finding correlations between them.
  4. A deep connection to humanity and the entire ecosystem.
  5. A felt sense of responsibility for self-care and others’ well-being.

My Alignment with IB

My experience and alignment with Global Perspectives, and my approach to student learning and their readiness for the world, go well with the core elements of the IBDP curriculum. My experience in understanding and connecting with each child — their thoughts, feelings and ideas — helps in accomplishing the child-centred approach required for CAS and EE.

Having completed my undergraduate in Aerospace Engineering and my Masters in Education, my grounding in mathematics, science and humanities keeps me ready to support students with any research topic, research methodology, conceptual understanding and interdisciplinary connections. I am always growing holistically and remain open to multiple cultures, perspectives and lifestyles — strongly believing in humanity and ecological well-being. These characteristics match the IB Learner Profile, and keep me ready to serve the IB curriculum with genuine commitment.
